pr_body:
In order to support additional media types in request body a custom
validation has to be supported.
This commit moves validation from RestController to RestHandler
interface (default) and allows new RestHandler implementations to
provide its custom implementation

closes #80482

pr_comments: Hi @pgomulka, I've created a changelog YAML for you.

@pgomulka On the original issue we discussed maintaining CSRF protection by continuing to reject any of the safelisted content types.

It doesn't look like this PR does that. Was that intentional?

great find @tvernum . It wasn't intentional, it was a while when I read the discussion and assumed the PR was ready.
I missed that the explicit check for XContentType values on Content-Type header was preventing the safelisted to be sent.. I will follow up in a new PR to fix this.
thanks again!

issue_context.title: Allow RestHandlers for Content-Type outside XContentType
issue_context.body:
It is currently impossible for `RestHandler` to deal with requests that specify a `Content-Type` that doesn't map to `XCotentType` due to strict validation inside `RestController.`
This makes dealing with binary data (for supporting endpoints/protocols that already exist) impossible since the handler never gets access to the underlying request - the sender receiving the response: `Content-Type header [<non-xcontent-type>] is not supported`

It would be great to allow the validation to be pluggable similar to the `Allow` header - a `RestHandler` could return its own `MediaTypeRegistry` to specify the accepted `Content-Type` (including requests without the header being defined).
comments:
we discussed this on 24th Nov on core infra sync
We have at the moment a homogenous view on what content type is supported in all our apis. A client supporting JSON, YAML, CBOR, SMILE has a guarantee that it can talk with any of the endpoints. 
A new api that do not parse our standard XContent media types will break that guarantee. @bytebilly wants to investigate a little more on this side.

Another concern was this would end up available for all plugins, which might be risky and need to keep this in mind.
We also need to find out if cloud proxy will be able to support a custom media type on content-type header.

Thanks @pgomulka for the great summary. Some additional context on the original reasons why this is enforced can be found here: https://www.elastic.co/blog/strict-content-type-checking-for-elasticsearch-rest-requests

I'd like to get some feedback on the following aspects:
- How is the content type handled in our language clients? In case we relax the constraint, would it be a simple way for developers to figure out which content type is allowed on a specific API without going to the documentation? Could language clients perform a per-api check to ensure that and warn developers if it's not the case? (@philkra)
- How could we prevent security implications? Are past concerns still valid and relevant today? Are new attacks possible if we relax this constraint? (@tvernum)
- how would it relate to Cloud? It's about our Cloud Proxy, but also other cloud-native common setups like service mesh. Is it something transparent to them, or should we care about implications? (@jowiho)

Unless we can get no concern by answering these questions, we'd probably need a strong benefit to move forward.
@costin I feel that having a concrete use case would really help to make a decision. Could you please share where the need is coming from?

cc @qhoxie

The _Cross Site Request Forgery_ issue is still relevant, but our content-type protection really only requires that the media type __not__ be any of the following
- `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`
- `multipart/form-data`
- `text/plain`

(Per: https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#cors-safelisted-request-header)

As long as the Rest server rejects those content types, our CSRF protection doesn't change.

> how would it relate to Cloud? It's about our Cloud Proxy, but also other cloud-native common setups like service mesh. Is it something transparent to them, or should we care about implications? 

As far as I know the Proxy doesn't care about the content type of ES requests (@igor-kupczynski please correct me if I'm overlooking something). Other Cloud services that connect to ES behave as regular clients, so they shouldn't be affected by a more relaxed content-type check.
Hey, ACK there should be no impact of changing ES requests `Content-Type`s on the cloud proxy.
@costin given the feedback above, I feel that there is no strong blocker if we can guarantee CSRF protection.

review_comments: Just for my own learning, was nobody using this interface method before? Do we need to still report somewhere that the default supported media type is MEDIA_TYPE_REGISTRY?

yes, it was not used. I added it in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/64406#issue-733110468 (see the description) but the validation of Accept header was never implemented. 
In fact, the `mediaTypesValid` added in this PR could be used for this.
The goal of this PR is to make it less strict though - to allow RestHandlers which intentionally want to implement their own `Content-Type` validation
